title: Franz Rosenzweig

Franz Rosenzweig

Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929) is considered a central axis in Western thought, representing the transition from absolute idealism to the religious existentialism and dialogical philosophy of the twentieth century. His foundational work, *Der Stern der Erlösung* (*The Star of Redemption*), presents a "new thinking" that begins with the individual's fear of death and rejects the Hegelian attempt to unify reality into a comprehensive system. Rosenzweig developed a theology of dual covenant, attributing equal redemptive legitimacy to Judaism ("the eternal fire") and Christianity ("the eternal rays"), and established the *Freies Jüdisches Lehrhaus* (*Free Jewish House of Study*) as a model for adult education aimed at directing modern Jews to return to their sources. Although his illness, ALS, physically paralyzed him, he continued to create, including within the framework of his pioneering Bible translation with Martin Buber, and to this day his thought influences thinkers such as Emmanuel Levinas and Leo Strauss.

The Critique of Hegelian Totalization

The "Old Thinking," according to Rosenzweig, was characterized by the desire to grasp "The All" (das All) through reason.[4, 5] From the Ionian pre-Socratics to Hegel, philosophy sought to eliminate the "Other" by absorbing God, Man, and World into a unified logical system.[3, 19] Rosenzweig argued that this systematic drive was "diseased" because it sought to "quench the cry of death" by reducing the unique, suffering individual to a mere moment in the development of Universal Spirit.[4, 20]

Rosenzweig's "New Thinking" (Das neue Denken) begins where philosophy traditionally ends: with the concrete individual's "fear of death".[4, 19, 21] Death is the ultimate fracture in any totalizing system; it is the point where the individual asserts their "I-I-I" against extinction.[4, 20] By accepting the finitude of human existence, the "New Thinking" moves from the monologue of abstract logic to the dialogue of "speech thinking" (Sprachdenken).[1, 4]

The Three Elements and Three Paths

The architecture of The Star of Redemption is built upon two interlocking triangles that form the Star of David.[1, 8, 22] The first triangle consists of the three primordial and irreducible elements of reality: God, World, and Man.[1, 15, 22]

God: Not a theological abstraction, but a metaphysical reality.[2, 16]

World: A pluriform, "metalogical" reality that cannot be reduced to human consciousness.[2, 23]

Man: A "metaethical" self, a solitary and mute individual who exists prior to any relation.[13, 23, 24]

The second triangle represents the "Paths" or relations that connect these elements, transforming the isolated "pre-cosmos" into a living reality [15, 24, 25]:

Creation (God-World): The act through which God affirms the world's existence.[15, 24] Creation is not a past event but an ongoing divine "Yes" to the physical universe.[15, 25]

Revelation (God-Man): The "beating heart" of the system.[24] Revelation is the moment when God addresses the individual in love.[15, 24] This address breaks the "mute" isolation of the self, awakening it into a "soul" that can speak and respond.[13, 23, 24]

Redemption (Man-World): The process by which the soul, empowered by divine love, turns toward the neighbor and the world.[15, 22] Redemption is the "ensouling" of the world through human acts of love and responsibility.[8, 15]

The Grammar of Eros and Speech Thinking

In Part II of The Star, Rosenzweig develops his "grammar of eros," using the Song of Songs as the paradigm for revelation.[23, 24] He rejects the idea that language is merely an analogy for divine truth; rather, language is the very medium of truth.[16, 23, 24] Revelation is a "speech event" where God's call—"Abraham, Abraham!"—meets the human response—"Here I am".[24] This dialogical structure establishes that selfhood is not a monologue but a response to being summoned by name.[4, 5, 24]

Rosenzweig's concept of "speech thinking" emphasizes the temporal and relational nature of existence.[1, 4] Unlike logical thinking, which is timeless and objective, speech requires a specific "Thou," a specific moment in time, and an openness to the future.[1, 4, 13] This philosophical shift had a profound impact on Martin Buber, although Rosenzweig critically engaged with Buber's "I-Thou" concept, arguing that Buber's "I-It" was too close to idealism.[8, 26] Rosenzweig proposed instead that the counterpart to "I-Thou" should be "He-It"—the world as God's creation, rather than an object of human cognition.[8]

Judaism and Christianity: The Eternal Fire and the Eternal Rays

One of the most radical and influential aspects of Rosenzweig's thought is his "dual covenant" theology, which grants equal redemptive legitimacy to both Judaism and Christianity.[2, 15, 27] He famously employs the metaphor of the Sun and its Rays to describe their relationship within the drama of redemption.[15, 28]

Judaism: The Fire at the Center

Rosenzweig portrays the Jewish people as the "eternal people" who live outside of world history.[2, 10, 28] By existing beyond the boundaries of specific states and the vicissitudes of political power, the Jews already dwell in a state of eternity.[2, 28] Their life is defined by the biological continuity of the "blood" and the cyclical pattern of the liturgical calendar.[15, 29]

The Liturgical Year: Festivals like Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot allow the Jew to "step out" of linear time and experience the redemptive future in the present moment.[4, 10, 15]

Non-Territoriality: Because Judaism is focused on the "eternal life" of the community rather than the "eternal way" of expansion, it eschews the need for a state.[15] This informed Rosenzweig's opposition to political Zionism, as he feared it would "embroil the Jews into a worldly history" that they had transcended.[8, 30]

Christianity: The Rays Reaching Outward

Christianity is described as the "eternal way," tasked with carrying the light of revelation to the "pagan" nations of the world.[15, 28] While the Jew is "already with the Father," the Christian is "ever on the way," transforming history and stripping it of its pagan foundations through proselytization and mission.[15, 28] The Christian mission is essential for the eventual redemption of the entire world, as it prepares the nations for the kingdom of God.[28]

Rosenzweig argues that Judaism and Christianity are interdependent. The living presence of the Jewish people serves as a "counterweight" to the pagan impulses within Christianity, preventing the Church from becoming a merely worldly institution.[10, 29] Conversely, the Christian mission ensures that the Jewish revelation reaches the farthest corners of the earth.[15, 28] Both are "laborers at the same task".[29]

The Freies Jüdisches Lehrhaus: A Renaissance of Jewish Learning

After the war, Rosenzweig moved to Frankfurt, where he sought to translate his philosophical insights into a practical pedagogical program. In October 192

0, he founded the Freies Jüdisches Lehrhaus (Free Jewish House of Study).[6, 12, 13] This institution was not a traditional university or a yeshiva, but an adult education center designed to bring "disengaged" Jews back to their heritage.[6, 12, 31]

## The Pedagogy of "Learning in Reverse"

Rosenzweig's educational philosophy, termed "New Learning," was based on the concept of the Center and Periphery.[6]

**The Old Way:** Traditionally, Jewish learning began at the "Center" (the Torah and the Law) and led outward into "Life".[6]

**The New Way:** In the modern, emancipated world, the "Center" had been lost to many Jews who lived on the "Periphery" (the world of secular professions and German culture).[6]

**The Mechanism:** Rosenzweig proposed a "reverse order" of learning: starting from the concrete experience of life—from the perspectives of the chemist, the physician, or the artist—and moving "backward" to the ancient sources.[6, 31]

The Lehrhaus was characterized by its intellectual diversity. Two-thirds of its teachers were from secular professions rather than the rabbinate.[6] Rosenzweig himself emphasized that "in being Jews we must not give up anything... but lead everything back to Judaism".[6] This approach allowed participants to foster a "dual identity"—to be both German and Jewish—by contextualizing their secular reality within a living Jewish dimension.[6] The Lehrhaus proved remarkably successful, enrolling over 1,100 students from a total Jewish population in Frankfurt of only 26,000.[31]

## Die Schrift: The Buber-Rosenzweig Bible Translation

In 1925, Rosenzweig embarked on one of his most ambitious projects: a collaborative German translation of the Hebrew Bible with Martin Buber.[1, 32, 33] Their goal was to produce a translation that was "authentically Jewish" while being accessible to a modern German audience, both Jewish and Christian.[33, 34]

### Methodology: Gesprochenheit and the Colon System

The translators rejected the standard literary German of their time, opting instead for a style that reflected the Gesprochenheit ("spokenness") of the original Hebrew.[32, 35] They believed the Bible was essentially an oral text—the "speaking voice of God"—and that the written word was merely a musical score for public recitation.[34]

**The Colon Principle:** The text was organized into cola (breathing units) rather than standard verses or paragraphs, mimicking the natural rhythm of a speaker.[33, 35]

**Root Repetition:** To capture the primordial meaning of the Hebrew, they intentionally retained the repetitive use of word roots, often creating new German compounds to mimic the idiosyncrasy of the original.[34]

**The Redactor as Rabbenu:** While acknowledging modern biblical scholarship (Higher Criticism), they viewed the final redactor (R) not as a mere editor but as "Moses our Teacher" (Rabbenu), the one who unified the various sources into a living whole for the community.[2, 7, 34]

### Translating the Divine Name

The translation of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) was perhaps their most distinctive contribution. Rather than using the traditional "Lord" (Herr), they used personal pronouns—Ich, Du, and Er (I, You, He)—that shifted depending on the speaker's perspective.[26, 36] For Rosenzweig, the divine name was not a static title but a declaration of God's "being-there-for" humanity, as revealed in the "I am that I am" of Exodus 3:14.[36]

## The Heroism of Suffering: ALS and the Late Years

In early 1922, Rosenzweig was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), an often fatal form of progressive paralysis.[1] The disease rapidly stripped him of his ability to move, speak, and breathe independently.[1, 8] Despite this catastrophic physical decline, Rosenzweig's intellectual clarity and spiritual vitality remained undiminished—a period often described as a "heroism of the spirit".[1]

With the help of his wife, Edith, Rosenzweig developed a painstaking method of communication.[8] Edith would recite the alphabet, and Rosenzweig would signal with a slight movement (eventually only a blink) when she reached the correct letter.[8] Later, he used a specialized typewriter plate to point to letters.[8] Through this method, he completed several volumes of the Bible translation, wrote numerous essays and record reviews, and maintained a vast correspondence.[1]

His final communication, dictated via the typewriter method, was a partial sentence regarding a revelation he received in his sleep: "And now it comes, the point of all points, which the Lord has truly revealed to me in my sleep, the point of all points for which there—".[8] The sentence was interrupted by his doctor, and Rosenzweig died on the night of December 10, 1929, in Frankfurt, at the age of 42.[1, 8]

## Legacy and Contemporary Influence

Franz Rosenzweig's influence on twentieth-century and contemporary thought is vast, extending into philosophy, theology, and political theory.

### Emmanuel Levinas: Totality and Infinity

Perhaps the most prominent heir to Rosenzweig's philosophy is Emmanuel Levinas.[23, 37, 38] Levinas explicitly acknowledged his debt to Rosenzweig in the preface to his masterpiece, Totality and Infinity (1961), stating that the opposition to the "idea of totality" in The Star was "too often present in this book to be cited".[23, 37]

**Responsibility for the Other:** Levinas expanded Rosenzweig's "speech thinking" into a radical ethics where the "Face of the Other" disrupts the ego's totality and imposes an inescapable responsibility.[19, 38, 39]

**Ethics as First Philosophy:** Following Rosenzweig, Levinas argued that ethics is not a derivative of metaphysics but the very foundation of all philosophical inquiry.[40, 41]

### Leo Strauss and Political Theology

Leo Strauss also confessed a significant debt to Rosenzweig, noting that Rosenzweig's return to Jewish revelation provided the impetus for his own critical examination of modern philosophy.[37] Strauss dedicated his first major book, Spinoza's Critique of Religion, to Rosenzweig'
